title: Commands and requests: from "kel" to "kelingiz"
goal: Tell, invite, offer, and forbid at the right level of politeness — the tools Uzbeks use most when hosting guests.
bekal: softening commands with *iltimos*, *marhamat*, and the suffix *-chi*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mehmon boʻling!
dialogs.intro: Budi visits Nilufar's family home for the first time. Nilufar's mother opens the door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. Here, a little gift.

lines.speaker: Ona:
lines.text: Voy, ovora boʻlmang! Kiring, oyoq kiyimni yeching.
lines.id: Oh, you shouldn't have! Come in, take off your shoes.
lines.literal: oh, bother don't-be! enter, foot clothing-(object) take-off.

lines.speaker: Ona:
lines.id: Take the seat of honor! Please come to the table.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Choy quyay. Koʻk choymi yoki qora choymi?
lines.id: Let me pour the tea. Green tea or black tea?
lines.literal: tea pour-I. green tea-? or black tea-?

lines.speaker: Ona:
lines.text: Nondan oling, uyalmang. Oshni ham torting.
lines.id: Have some bread, don't be shy. Try the plov too.
lines.literal: bread-from take, don't-be-shy. plov-(object) also pull.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: It's delicious! Could I have the recipe?

lines.speaker: Ona:
lines.text: Albatta. Lekin avval yeng, keyin yozing!
lines.id: Of course. But eat first, write later!
lines.literal: of-course. but first eat, then write!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Xoʻp boʻladi. Yana keling deb aytmang — men oʻzim kelaman!
lines.id: All right. Don't tell me "come again" — I'll come on my own!
lines.literal: OK becomes. again come saying don't-say — I myself come-I!

notes: **Keling is said twice, and on purpose.** Repeating a command is how Uzbek warms it up: *keling-keling*, *oling-oling*, *mayli-mayli*. Once sounds like an order; twice sounds like a welcome.
**Toʻr is the seat of honor** — the side of the room farthest from the door. Guests are guided there, and refusing it only troubles the host. If you're told *toʻrga oʻting*, just go.
**Dasturxon** isn't a table but the cloth spread out with food — and also the name for the whole meal. *Dasturxonga marhamat* is the most typical invitation to eat.

**Ovora boʻlmang = "don't go to any trouble".** Paired with *uyalmang* (don't be shy), these are must-know phrases for any guest in Uzbekistan. The host will keep offering; refusing once is seen as politeness, so if you're really full, say *rahmat, toʻydim* (thank you, I'm full).

grammars.title: Three levels of command, and one invitation
body: The basic form is the bare verb stem — no ending at all. Politeness is added from there.
after: **Use -ing until you're really sure.** The bare form sounds rude to people you've just met, and there's no harm in sounding a little too polite.
The last row is very handy: *Choy quyay* (let me pour the tea), *Kiray?* (may I come in?), *Koʻray* (let me see). The *-ay* form is the gentlest way to offer yourself.
⚠️ Stems ending in a vowel insert *-y-*: *oʻqi-* → *oʻqi**y**ing*, *ishla-* → *ishla**y**ing*. And *-ing* on stems ending in *-k/-q* softens them: *yoq-* → *yoqing*, but *toʻk-* → *toʻking*.

grammars.title: Forbidding, and softening
body: A prohibition uses the same *-ma-* as an ordinary negative, inserted before the command ending.
after: **-chi is the most typically Uzbek softener.** It turns a command into a friendly request: *Bering* (give) → *Bering-chi* (could I have it?). The closest English is a friendly "go on" or a tag like "would you?".
*Iltimos* can go before or after: *Iltimos, kuting* or *Kuting, iltimos*. Both are equally polite.
For a gentler prohibition, the *kerak emas* form is used: *Bormasangiz ham boʻladi* (it's fine if you don't go). That form waits for unit 18; for now *-mang* covers every situation.

sections.title: Being a guest in an Uzbek home

blocks.text: Hosting guests in Uzbekistan isn't extra friendliness but a duty seen as sacred. There's a proverb: *Mehmon otangdan ulugʻ* — "a guest is greater than your father". These ten sentences cover a whole first visit.

blocks.text: The two blessings in the middle of the table — *Qoʻlingiz dard koʻrmasin* and *Uyingiz obod boʻlsin* — use the *-sin* form, a command for the third person ("may it…"). It isn't taught as grammar in this book; just learn them whole, and people will be impressed.
Vocabulary you'll use the moment you're invited.

A *piyola* is a handleless tea bowl, and pouring it has its own rules: the host fills it **only a third of the way**. It isn't stinginess — the more often they pour, the more often they attend to you, and that's the respect. A full bowl actually means "time to go home".
⚠️ *Hammom* (bathroom) is a cousin of Turkish "hamam" and Arabic "hammam". But if you're looking for the toilet, the right word is *hojatxona* or, in public places, simply *tualet*.
